title: Papyrus graecus holmiensis (P. holm.); Recepte für Silber, Steine und Purpur
venue: Uppsala/Leipzig: A.-B. Akademiska Bokhandeln / Harrassowitz (scan on Internet Archive)
ask_addressed: What textual and material evidence shows alchemy / early chemistry in Greco-Roman Egypt (Alexandria, Panopolis): Leiden papyrus X, Stockholm papyrus, Pseudo-Democritus Physika kai Mystika, Zosimus of Panopolis, Mary the Jewess (Maria Prophetissa) and her apparatus, Cleopatra the Alchemist? Dates, languages, and what they actually describe (practical dye/metal recipes versus theory).
quote: P. Holm. ist eine Sammlung chemischer Recepte.
summary: Editio princeps of the Stockholm papyrus (Greek text, German translation, commentary). Lagercrantz treats it as craft recipes compiled over generations, and in the same work analyses Pseudo-Democritus' Physika kai Mystika as three unconnected parts: purple recipes 'rein technischen, also nicht alchimistischen Charakter', a necromantic episode, and alchemical gold/silver recipes; he states the real Democritus had nothing to do with it.
limits: A 1913 edition; later work (Halleux 1981, not opened) supersedes its dating and readings. OCR text of the scan was read, not the plates. It discusses Leiden X but does not date Pseudo-Democritus precisely ('fehlen alle Stützpunkte').

title: Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs, Première livraison (Introduction; Les papyrus de Leide)
venue: Paris: Steinheil (scan on Internet Archive, University of Toronto copy)
ask_addressed: What textual and material evidence shows alchemy / early chemistry in Greco-Roman Egypt (Alexandria, Panopolis): Leiden papyrus X, Stockholm papyrus, Pseudo-Democritus Physika kai Mystika, Zosimus of Panopolis, Mary the Jewess (Maria Prophetissa) and her apparatus, Cleopatra the Alchemist? Dates, languages, and what they actually describe (practical dye/metal recipes versus theory).
quote: il remonte à la fin du troisième siècle de notre ère, d'après Reuvens et Leemans.
summary: Berthelot's 1887 introduction describes Leiden papyrus X (found at Thebes) as a set of 101 chemistry/alchemy recipes plus 10 extracts from Dioscorides, dated by its editors to the end of the 3rd century CE; he calls it the oldest manuscript on such subjects then known and a source of metal-alloy and colouring practice (gold and silver imitation).
limits: A nineteenth-century reading; Berthelot calls the papyrus 'les carnets d'un artisan faussaire', an inference. Dating is by Reuvens/Leemans' palaeography as he reports it, not his own measurement.

title: Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs, Seconde livraison: Les œuvres de Zosime
ask_addressed: Is there any evidence for alchemy in pharaonic Egypt before the Ptolemies? State what is absent as well as what is present.
quote: Cet art divin a été révélé aux prêtres seuls
summary: In Zosimus' Final Account (Livre du Compte final, to Theosebeia), as translated by Berthelot, the 'king of Egypt' practised these arts and the divine art was revealed to priests only. This is the late-3rd/4th-century claim of a priestly Egyptian origin; the same volume contains the passage 'two sciences and two wisdoms, that of the Egyptians and that of the Hebrews'.
limits: A claim by an author writing around 300 CE, not contemporary pharaonic evidence. Berthelot's translation is old; Mertens' 1995 edition (not opened) is standard. Stance lowered from supports to context by verifier: the page shows only Zosimus' late claim of priestly Egyptian origin, which is not evidence for pharaonic-period alchemy.

title: Ancient handbooks and Graeco-Egyptian collections of alchemical recipes
venue: BJHS Themes 5, 39-55 (Cambridge University Press, open access CC BY 4.0)
ask_addressed: What textual and material evidence shows alchemy / early chemistry in Greco-Roman Egypt (Alexandria, Panopolis): Leiden papyrus X, Stockholm papyrus, Pseudo-Democritus Physika kai Mystika, Zosimus of Panopolis, Mary the Jewess (Maria Prophetissa) and her apparatus, Cleopatra the Alchemist? Dates, languages, and what they actually describe (practical dye/metal recipes versus theory).
quote: two anonymous recipe books on papyrus codices written in third- or fourth-century Egypt
summary: Martelli describes the Leiden and Stockholm papyri as recipe books (over 200 recipes: metal colouring, gold- and silver-coloured alloys, inks, fake gems, purple wool) linked to workshop practice, and argues that Zosimus' Syriac texts show earlier recipe books circulating under the title encheiridion.
limits: Focused on ancient recipe handbooks and Zosimus' sources, not an overview of origins. Dating is given as a range (3rd or 4th century). Does not address pharaonic Egypt in the pages read. Quote's 'fourth-century' is hyphenated across a line break in the PDF text.

title: The Visions of Zosimos of Panopolis: Text, Translation, and Commentary (introduction, on defining Graeco-Egyptian alchemy)
venue: DPhil thesis, University of Oxford (Oxford Research Archive)
ask_addressed: What textual and material evidence shows alchemy / early chemistry in Greco-Roman Egypt (Alexandria, Panopolis): Leiden papyrus X, Stockholm papyrus, Pseudo-Democritus Physika kai Mystika, Zosimus of Panopolis, Mary the Jewess (Maria Prophetissa) and her apparatus, Cleopatra the Alchemist? Dates, languages, and what they actually describe (practical dye/metal recipes versus theory).
quote: Early Greco-Egyptian alchemy (first through fourth centuries CE) is a craft (technē) rooted in ancient artisanal traditions involving the coloration of metals.
summary: Quoting Grimes (2022), Werrett gives the working definition; he dates the Leiden and Stockholm papyri 250-300 CE, places Ps.-Democritus' Physika kai Mystika among 1st-3rd century texts, and summarises three views of Zosimus' career (client scholar; temple metallurgist-priest; temple workshop member).
limits: A doctoral thesis, not peer-reviewed publication. Quotes Grimes's definition rather than stating its own. Says there is 'no direct evidence' Zosimos visited Dendera, so the temple-workshop reading is hypothesis.

title: Alchemy (Wikipedia; history, Hellenistic Egypt)
ask_addressed: Is there any evidence for alchemy in pharaonic Egypt before the Ptolemies? State what is absent as well as what is present.
quote: there is little to no evidence for his assertion
summary: The article says Zosimus asserted that alchemy dated back to pharaonic Egypt where it was the domain of the priestly class, and gives the assessment that there is little to no evidence; it also reports recent scholarship stressing Zosimus's link to Egyptian temple metallurgy and ceremony.
limits: Tertiary. The sentence is footnoted but the support was not traced. Use only as a pointer; weigh against Werrett and Martelli.

title: Leyden papyrus X (Wikipedia)
ask_addressed: What textual and material evidence shows alchemy / early chemistry in Greco-Roman Egypt (Alexandria, Panopolis): Leiden papyrus X, Stockholm papyrus, Pseudo-Democritus Physika kai Mystika, Zosimus of Panopolis, Mary the Jewess (Maria Prophetissa) and her apparatus, Cleopatra the Alchemist? Dates, languages, and what they actually describe (practical dye/metal recipes versus theory).
quote: The presentation is exclusively practical, and does not include the usual alchemical or philosophical elements.
summary: Summarises the papyrus as 10 leaves with 111 recipes (extracting or counterfeiting precious metals and stones, purple dye, inks), the last eleven being extracts from Dioscorides. The recipes are terse and probably served as an aide-memoire.
limits: Tertiary. Matches Berthelot's count (101 + 10) but Halleux 1981 and Caley 1926 were not opened.
